note.note:
Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 32-year-old male plastic-surgery doctor with 1.5–2 months of recurrent right-sided sensory and motor episodes; GP impression is probable transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) → urgent referral to TIA clinic.

History:
• Presenting complaint & timeline  
  - Episodic pins-and-needles/numbness in right hand, subjective weakness in right arm and right leg with colleague-noticed gait change.  
  - Episodes initially once / week → now several times per day; each lasts “few days” then resolves completely; asymptomatic at time of call.  
  - Newer episode features: difficulty holding coffee cup, transient throat “something there” sensation. No dysarthria, no visual disturbance.  
• Associated symptoms: fatigue, intermittent nausea during episodes. Denies ongoing swallowing difficulty or speech problems.  
• Pertinent negatives: no headache, no loss of consciousness, no chest pain, no known cardiac disease.  
• Past medical history: none reported.  
• Medications: Aspirin 75 mg daily (self-initiated).  
• Allergies: Penicillin.  
• Family history: Father underwent carotid endarterectomy for stroke prevention.  
• Social / preventive: Non-smoker, lives with wife, works as physician (plastic surgery). No alcohol or recreational drug use mentioned.

Examination:
• Remote video consult; no vitals recorded.  
• Patient alert, fluent speech, no visible focal deficit during call.  
• No physical examination performed.

Impression:
• Working diagnosis: Recurrent transient ischemic attacks (TIA) – unilateral episodic sensory-motor deficits, positive family history; GP pursuing urgent evaluation.  
• Alternate considerations (per DDx and symptom pattern):  
  1. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis – age-appropriate; episodes lasting days with mixed sensory/motor and bulbar features.  
  2. Cervical or central structural lesion (e.g., cord compression, demyelinating or vascular malformation).  
  Rationale: Episodes exceed 24 h (not classic TIA) and increasing frequency; however vascular cause prioritized due to unilateral nature and family history.

Plan:
• Urgent referral to hospital TIA clinic within 24–48 h for:  
  - Carotid Doppler ultrasound.  
  - Brain imaging (likely MRI/CT) ± additional vascular studies.  
• Provide clinic and PALS contact numbers; patient to phone if appointment not arranged promptly.  
• Safety-net: If symptoms recur and are prolonged or new deficits appear, attend Emergency Department immediately.  
• Continue aspirin 75 mg daily for now; discuss long-term antiplatelet need after specialist review.  
• GP to document referral and contact details in record.

Quality checks:

● Missing / expected elements: vitals, objective neurologic exam, alcohol use, full medication list confirmation, vaccination/ preventive status, explicit follow-up appointment date.  
● Conflicts: Episode duration (“few days”) conflicts with classic TIA definition (<24 h); noted but GP still pursuing TIA pathway.  
● Transcript quality: Audio interruptions, loss of video, some ambiguity on episode frequency and duration; otherwise coherent history.
